wine.name: Kéknyelű
wine.grapes: Kéknyelű, the blue stalked native white of the Badacsony hills, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: Kéknyelű on the basalt of Badacsony hill above the lake, and part of the last old plot of the grape at Nemesgulács, which the founder bought when the variety was saved, by Magyar Bor's account.
wine.making: The house's own cellar notes could not be read, so no vessel is claimed. Magyar Bor says Kéknyelű is mostly made dry and often given long time in bottle, and that barrel ageing suits it too; the grape flowers as a female, so a pollinating variety grows beside it and is picked and made apart.
wine.glass: Lean and taut: green apple, lime peel and bitter almond over a smoky, stony, saline edge from the basalt, with high, firm acidity and a long, narrow finish that opens slowly with air and age.
wine.ageing: Closed and austere in its first years; its high acidity, the trait that gives the grape its name for long life, lets a good bottle keep and open for many years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: Blue stalk: the grape is named for the faint blue tint of its leaf stalks.
The protected wine district around the basalt hill on the northern shore of Lake Balaton.

records.table: Szeremley is the Badacsonytomaj estate whose founder helped save Kéknyelű, the blue stalked native white of the Balaton hills, after 1990. Its Kéknyelű is lean, smoky and high in acid, slow to open, so pour it cool and give it air.
records.story: Huba Szeremley (1940 to 2021) was born in Budapest and left Hungary in 1967, building a fortune abroad. By one account the summers of his childhood by Lake Balaton drew him back after the change of regime, and in the 1990s he pieced together a large holding of vineyard land on the Badacsony hills. Kéknyelű, the hills' own white grape, had shrunk after phylloxera and almost vanished in the socialist years, when even the state's collection of the variety was grubbed up; a few thousand vines survived, the last old plot of them at Nemesgulács. With other growers he set about saving it: cuttings were taken from that plot, which he bought in part, and the grape was planted again. It is a hard vine to grow, with only female flowers, so a pollinating variety must stand beside it, and it sets small, uneven bunches. By the time he died in May 2021, Kéknyelű was planted again across the district, and his part in the revival is told by the national wine body and by the wine press alike. In his last years much of his estate was sold at auction, but the cellar at Badacsonytomaj kept his name. For a sommelier, Szeremley's Kéknyelű is where the story of the grape's return begins.

wine.name: Szürkebarát
wine.grapes: Szürkebarát, the Hungarian name for Pinot Gris, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the basalt witness hills of the lake, whose main parcels lie on Badacsony and Csobánc, by the house's account; the house does not name the parcels of this bottling.
wine.making: Made dry in the house's cellar at Badacsony, by its own account with a drop of residual sugar left in to round the wine; its notes give no vessel or ageing, so none is claimed here.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, acacia blossom and a hint of white pepper, full and round in the mouth, softened by the touch of sweetness the house leaves; richer than a Pinot Grigio and closer to Alsace in weight, as Badacsony's Szürkebarát runs.
wine.ageing: Drink it young, within a few years of the vintage, while its pear and blossom are fresh; the house gives no ageing advice of its own.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a medium white wine glass.

records.table: Laposa is a Badacsony family estate grown from a wedding present of 1978, a small press house above the lake. Its Szürkebarát is Pinot Gris in Badacsony's fuller way, pear and acacia blossom with a touch of sweetness, closer to Alsace than to Pinot Grigio.
records.story: The house tells its story from 1978, when two families met in marriage at the Hableány, an old hotel by the lake: the Laposas of Budapest, who were coopers, and the Barabás family of Badacsony, who grew vines. The young couple were given a small press house in the Balaton Uplands as a wedding present, and the family spent more and more time there. Magyar Bor's register gives 1990 as the founding of the estate; from the early 1990s it grew, choosing land across the Badacsony wine district, with its main parcels on Badacsony itself and on Csobánc, and by the house's own account its first vines were planted in 1992 and the Istenmeredekje vineyard in 1994. The next generation took the estate on from its parents more than a decade ago, and in 2019 the Hableány, where the founders had married, was restored as the estate's centre. Laposa works almost wholly in white wine and in the district's own grapes: Olaszrizling, Rajnai Rizling, Kéknyelű, Furmint and Szürkebarát, which Magyar Bor counts with Olaszrizling and Kéknyelű among Badacsony's three traditional leading varieties. Its Szürkebarát shows what that historic grape gives on basalt by the lake: a fuller, rounder Pinot Gris than the Italian style.

report: The plan's doubt stands in part: no source names a flagship of the house. A plain Szürkebarát is on the house's own shop (the Vitorlás Szürkebarát, and earlier a Laposa Szürkebarát), and Szürkebarát is one of its five main grapes, so the record keeps the wine under the thin region rule; the PiNO, the house's more serious Pinot Gris, is among the others. A rename to the PiNO was weighed and not proposed: one critic calls it a blend of several Pinots, and the house's pages disagree on its vineyard (a south slope before the terrace, or Istenmeredekje, planted 1994).
Founded is Magyar Bor's 1990; the house tells the 1978 wedding and first vines in 1992, both in the story as the house's account.
Whether this bottling carries Badacsony or the wider Balatoni designation could not be confirmed on a label; Badacsony stands on two retail listings.

The making and the glass rest on the house's product notes (pear, white flowers, gentle spice, full, a drop of residual sugar) and Magyar Bor's description of Badacsony Szürkebarát as Alsatian in weight; no vessel or ageing is claimed.
The grey friar meaning of Szürkebarát is the plain translation of the word; the legend of monks bringing the grape found no source and is left out.
The living owners named on the house's and Magyar Bor's pages are not named; the founders' first names and the book about the father are left out.

wine.name: Rajnai Rizling
wine.grapes: Rajnai Rizling, Rhine Riesling, alone: the estate grows no other grape.
wine.sites: South facing vineyards in the core of Badacsony hill, among them parcels of the former Esterházy and Ranolder estates; the Kezdet vineyard, very stony and rich in basalt, gives the single vineyard wines.
wine.making: Yields are kept low and the harvest is drawn late into the season, by the house's account. Press fractions and parcels are fermented apart in steel tanks and the wines are blended from tank; the single vineyard wines are fermented and matured in steel, and fermentation is at times stopped with a little sugar left.
wine.glass: Lime, green apple and white peach over a smoky, stony note of the basalt, with Riesling's high, firm acidity and, in some cuvées, a trace of sweetness to balance it.
wine.ageing: Approachable young; Riesling's high acidity lets the stonier single vineyard wines keep longer, though the house gives no figure.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a young bottle; a white wine glass with a narrow rim.

label.means: Rhine Riesling, the true Riesling, under its Hungarian name.

records.table: Villa Sandahl is the Badacsony estate founded by Swedes in 2004 that grows one grape only, Rajnai Rizling, the true Riesling. Its Rieslings, fermented apart by parcel in steel, set lime and green apple against the smoky stone of the basalt hill.
records.story: Villa Sandahl began in 2004, when two Swedish founders of the Sandahl family and their families bought vineyards on Badacsony hill. By their own account they chose Hungary because vineyards of real quality could then be bought by private wine lovers, and the slopes they found were south facing, at the core of the hill, among them land of the former Esterházy and Ranolder estates. Those slopes proved a little too warm for early ripening grapes, so the founders settled on Rajnai Rizling, Rhine Riesling, which ripens late and keeps its acidity, and head grafted or replanted their vines to it. The estate grows nothing else, and every wine is a Riesling, given its own name by vintage, parcel or pressing, and the house keeps yields low and picks late. In the cellar the press fractions and the parcels are fermented apart in steel tanks and the wines are blended from tank, the stoniest, from the basalt of the Kezdet vineyard, kept apart as single vineyard wines under the Rare Peak name. In May 2016 the estate opened a guesthouse, the Sandahl Rezidencia, and in 2024 it marked its twentieth year. For a sommelier, Villa Sandahl is the plain case for Riesling on Badacsony basalt, in a district better known for Olaszrizling.

wine.name: Csobáncz Olaszrizling
wine.grapes: Olaszrizling, Welschriesling, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards at the foot of Csobánc, a volcanic witness hill north of the lake, where a topsoil weathered from basalt lies over a rare layer of calcareous sand.
wine.making: By the house's own account the must settles naturally for at most twelve hours, then ferments spontaneously in steel tanks or in 500 litre Stockinger casks; the wine stays long on its yeast, is first racked after three to four months, and is given little sulphur.
wine.glass: Lemon peel, green apple and almond, with ripe peach and a salty edge on the finish; dry and firm, with the bitter almond close that marks Olaszrizling and a tight, stony line.
wine.ageing: Good young and fresh; its acidity carries it for several years, though the house gives no figure.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a medium white wine glass.

records.table: Villa Tolnay is the estate on Csobánc, a volcanic hill behind Badacsony, named for the actress whose weekend house it was. Its Csobáncz Olaszrizling is dry, firm and salty, lemon and almond from basalt soil over calcareous sand, wild fermented and long on its lees.
records.story: The house at the foot of Csobánc was the weekend retreat of Klári Tolnay (1914 to 1998), an actress of the Hungarian stage and screen, who spent her free time on the hill behind Badacsony. In 2004 a Swiss wine lover bought her former villa, drawn by the view from the hill, and founded a winery there, keeping her name for it. The estate grew steadily from that start, almost all of it on Csobánc, one of the volcanic witness hills that rise from the Tapolca basin north of the lake, where basalt weathers into a topsoil that lies over calcareous sand. The house grows both Rieslings, Rajnai Rizling and Olaszrizling, with Furmint, Zöldveltelini and a few red grapes, and makes its wines by a rule of its own: a short natural settling of the must, a spontaneous ferment in steel or in large Austrian casks, a long time on the yeast and little sulphur. Its first sparkling wine, a Furmint, came with the 2020 vintage. The Csobáncz Olaszrizling, labelled under the wider Balatoni name with the hill's old spelling, is the house's word on the Balaton's everyday grape: the same Olaszrizling as Csopak's, given the structure of a volcanic hill.

wine.name: Lőczedombi Olaszrizling
wine.grapes: Olaszrizling, Welschriesling, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: Lőczedomb, a single vineyard on the slopes of Lőcze hill above Csopak, on thick red Permian sandstone, the soil that marks the district east of Csopak.
wine.making: For the 2024 vintage, by Magyar Bor's notes, half was fermented spontaneously and aged for four months in 225 litre French barrels and half fermented and aged in steel tanks before the two were brought together; the share may move with the vintage.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon peel and bitter almond, the almond close of Olaszrizling, with a light toast from the barrel half and a salty, fine boned line from the red sandstone.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of the vintage; its acidity carries it for several years more, though the house gives no figure.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a medium white wine glass.

records.table: Jásdi is the Csopak house on the old wine estate of a nineteenth century bishop of Veszprém. Its Lőczedombi Olaszrizling comes from red Permian sandstone on Lőcze hill, half in French barrels, half in steel: green apple, almond and a salty line.
records.story: János Ranolder (1806 to 1875), Bishop of Veszprém from 1850, began buying land at Csopak in 1853 and built a wine estate there in stages, one that helped put the village on the wine map; he died at Csopak. After him the estate declined for half a century, and by the 1990s it was close to a ruin. In 1998 the Jásdi family took it on and rebuilt it, and the old press house became their cellar. They named their Olaszrizling and Furmint cuvée Ranolder White for the bishop, since that pairing of the two grapes was a traditional Csopak way of joining their strengths. In 2012 a group of Csopak producers created the Csopak Codex, a mark for wines of Olaszrizling alone from twenty six protected vineyards, and Jásdi's Lőczedombi Olaszrizling of 2013 was chosen as a Codex wine. Lőczedomb lies on Lőcze hill above the village, on the thick red Permian sandstone that marks the land east of Csopak, a soil quite unlike the basalt of Badacsony. Csopak lies in the Balatonfüred-Csopak district, not in Badacsony, and Jásdi stands here as the Balaton's sandstone answer to the basalt hills: the same grape, a different stone.

report: The plan's merge read is borne out: Csopak lies in the Balatonfüred-Csopak district, not Badacsony, and the record says so plainly. A swap is proposed for the checker: a house of the Badacsony district itself, Istvándy of Káptalantóti (its own Kéknyelű, a Kéknyelű sparkling wine first shown in 2012, by its own account) or the Borbély estate, both named by Magyar Bor among Badacsony's Kéknyelű makers; either would need its own research, and Istvándy would double Szeremley's grape.
The bishop's dates rest on Catholic Hierarchy (born 16 May 1806, died 12 September 1875 at Csopak, Bishop of Veszprém from 1850) and the purchases from 1853 on the Csopak village heritage study.
The family's start in 1998 rests on Magyar Bor's register and a Balaton tourism profile; one writer's profile says the estate was bought in 2002, perhaps a later stage, and is not followed.

The 2013 Lőczedombi as a Codex wine rests on one regional report (We Love Balaton, 2014) and is told without hedge only because the Codex itself is on Magyar Bor's district page; the checker should test it.
The plan's old vines are left out for want of a source; the making is the 2024 vintage's as Magyar Bor's notes give it, and said so.
Whether the label carries the Balatonfüred-Csopak name or Csopaki could not be confirmed; the appellation field gives the district.
The living founder and family are not named.
